findings.title: Unauthenticated file read via plugin UI static route
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugin-ui-static.ts:228 (GET /_plugins/:pluginId/ui/*filePath), mounted at server/src/app.ts:276 with no auth middleware.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller on the network (in `authenticated` deployments the privateHostnameGuard only runs when deploymentExposure is "private", app.ts:126-138, and actorMiddleware only populates req.actor — it never rejects) crossing into the server's filesystem, reading plugin files it has no account for.
Path: req.params.pluginId -> registry.getById/getByKey (no caller scoping, plugin-registry.ts:66-80) -> plugin.status must be "ready" -> manifest.entrypoints.ui -> resolvePluginUiDir -> path.resolve(uiDir, rawFilePath) -> realpath containment check (lines 411-438, which does block ../ and symlink escapes) -> res.sendFile(resolvedFilePath, { dotfiles: "allow" }).
Why nothing stops it: the file contains no assertBoard/requireBoard/req.actor check at all, unlike every sibling route (routes/plugins.ts:374, 443, 604, 796, 963, 1042, 1123, 1201, ...). The only gates are `plugin.status === "ready"` and `manifest.entrypoints.ui`; the plugin key form of :pluginId (e.g. paperclip-kitchen-sink-example) makes the ids guessable, and `dotfiles: "allow"` also serves dot-files/dot-directories inside the declared UI dir. The same handler additionally reaches the loopback dev-proxy fetch at line 358 unauthenticated whenever a plugin has devUiUrl configured and NODE_ENV !== "production" (the production check at line 293 only logs and falls through).
Impact: anyone who can reach the server downloads installed plugins' UI bundles and any other artifact the plugin ships under its declared UI directory (source maps, .env/config files when a plugin declares a broad entrypoints.ui such as "./" or "./dist/"), and can drive/read the configured loopback dev-server through the proxy — with no account and no audit identity.
Fix: enforce the same board guard the other plugin routes use (e.g. `assertBoard(req)` / `req.actor.type === "board"`) at the top of the handler before the registry lookup and sendFile; the browser's dynamic import of the bundle carries the session cookie so this keeps working. Gate the devUiUrl proxy branch behind board + instance-admin as well.

findings.title: Board user of one company can read any company's plugin data via params.companyId
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:962 (POST /api/plugins/:pluginId/data/:key; identical at :795 bridge/data, :878 bridge/action, :1041 actions/:key) — the handler forwards `params` to the worker verbatim and validates only the separate top-level `body.companyId` via assertCompanyAccess (routes/plugins.ts:995-997).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who is a member of company A only, crossing into company B's data through any installed plugin.
Path: body `{"params": {"companyId": "<company B>", "projectId": "<B project>"}}` with no top-level companyId -> assertCompanyAccess is never invoked (it is bound to body.companyId, which the worker never receives) -> workerManager.call(plugin.id, "getData", { key, params }) -> plugin handler takes the id from params (packages/plugins/examples/plugin-file-browser-example/src/worker.ts:82,97,113,151,180: `const companyId = typeof params.companyId === "string" ? params.companyId : ""`) -> ctx.projects.listWorkspaces / ctx.issues.list({ companyId }) -> this file's ensureCompanyId(params.companyId) (line 467) and inCompany/requireInCompany (lines 499-513) validate the record against the *caller-supplied* id, and ensurePluginAvailableForCompany (line 497) is an empty function, so even a company-level plugin disable in plugin_company_settings is never enforced.
Why nothing stops it: the host never carries the initiating user's identity into buildHostServices — only the pluginId/pluginKey are bound at construction (app.ts:243), so every method here treats `params.companyId` as authoritative, and the one user-facing check (assertCompanyAccess) is applied to a different field than the one the data access uses.
Impact: cross-tenant read of company-scoped records (projects, workspaces/workspace paths, issues, goals, agents, activity) by any user of any company, and for action keys potentially cross-tenant writes, via any plugin that forwards UI params to host services.
Fix: derive the company scope from the authenticated actor in the bridge handlers (never from the request body) and pass it to the worker as a host-controlled RPC field, have buildHostServices reject any params.companyId that does not match that per-call scope, and implement ensurePluginAvailableForCompany against plugin_company_settings so a company's disable actually blocks data access.

findings.title: Authenticated user executes arbitrary code via plugin manifest import
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:603 (POST /api/plugins/install, guarded only by assertBoard at line 604, body {packageName, version, isLocalPath}).
Attacker: any authenticated board user (a company member with no instance-admin role, or any invited user in an authenticated deployment), crossing from ordinary application user into operator/administrator power by getting code to execute in the Paperclip server process.
Path: routes/plugins.ts:641 loader.installPlugin({packageName: trimmedPackage, version}) -> plugin-loader.ts:835 execFileAsync("npm", ["install", spec, ...]) installs the caller-named package (--ignore-scripts blocks npm lifecycle hooks) -> line 868 resolveManifestPath(resolvedPackagePath, pkgJson) -> line 875 loadManifestFromPath -> line 930 `await import(manifestPath)` loads and executes the package's manifest module (e.g. dist/manifest.js) inside the host process before any capability validation; only afterwards does line 939 manifestValidator.parseOrThrow(raw) validate the shape of what was already executed.
Why nothing stops it: the only checks on the way are assertBoard (authentication, not authorization — assertInstanceAdmin exists in routes/authz.ts and is used for the devUiUrl config field at routes/plugins.ts:1563 but not for install) and the npm package-name character check at routes/plugins.ts:631, which constrains the spec string but not the code inside the package. The plugin runtime's real sandbox is the worker process plus capability-gated host services (buildHostServices / createHostClientHandlers), and the manifest import happens in the host process outside that sandbox, so a plugin that would be limited to a few host capabilities once running already has unconstrained code execution at install time.
Impact: a low-privileged authenticated user can publish (or point isLocalPath at) a package whose manifest module reads the server's filesystem, the database credentials and plugin secrets, or spawns processes, i.e. full compromise of the host running Paperclip.
Fix: require instance-admin (assertInstanceAdmin) for POST /api/plugins/install and for upgrade/uninstall, and load the manifest as data rather than code — parse manifest.json (or import it in a child process / worker with no host privileges and no ambient credentials) instead of `import()`-ing an arbitrary module in the server process.

findings.title: Authenticated user deletes arbitrary server directories via unvalidated plugin package name
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1230 (DELETE /api/plugins/:pluginId) -> server/src/services/plugin-lifecycle.ts:544/564 (pluginLoaderInstance.cleanupInstallArtifacts(plugin)), fed by the packageName stored when a plugin was installed through POST /api/plugins/install (routes/plugins.ts:637-639: for isLocalPath installs the stored name comes unvalidated from the installed directory's package.json "name" field, plugin-loader.ts:813-816).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who installed a plugin, crossing from plugin management into deleting arbitrary directories on the server host.
Path: plugin-loader.ts:1387 `const managedNodeModulesDir = resolveManagedInstallPackageDir(localPluginDir, plugin.packageName)` -> line 1942-1947 `path.join(localPluginDir, "node_modules", packageName)`, where packageName may contain "/" and ".." -> line 1390 `managedTargets.add(managedNodeModulesDir)` with no containment check -> line 1419-1421 `for (const target of managedTargets) { if (!existsSync(target)) continue; await rm(target, { recursive: true, force: true }); }`.
Why nothing stops it: the same function applies isPathInsideDir() to directManagedDir (line 1391) and to plugin.packagePath (line 1394) but not to the npm-managed directory built from plugin.packageName, and path.join normalizes ".." so a name such as "../../../../../srv/data" resolves outside localPluginDir and is then recursively force-deleted; nothing validates pkgJson.name or plugin.packageName against a package-name grammar at install time or before deletion.
Impact: removal of arbitrary directories readable/writable by the server process (databases' data dirs, worktrees, user data) triggered by a plugin uninstall/disable.
Fix: validate the package name at install time against the npm name grammar (no path separators, no ".."), and in cleanupInstallArtifacts run every managed target through isPathInsideDir(target, localPluginDir) (or resolve the managed directory with resolveManagedInstallPackageDir plus a containment assertion) before adding it to managedTargets or calling rm().

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF: plugin dev proxy follows redirects to internal hosts
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugin-ui-static.ts:228 — GET /_plugins/:pluginId/ui/*filePath, mounted at app level in server/src/app.ts:276 (outside /api, so no boardMutationGuard and no assertBoard anywhere in the handler).
Attacker: any unauthenticated client that can reach the server port (or any web page, since the route is a plain GET with no auth), crossing from the public HTTP surface into the server's loopback network and the developer's local-only services, and — via the redirect below — into internal/metadata addresses.
Path: req.params.filePath -> rawFilePath (line 234-237) -> decode/scheme checks (lines 306-320) -> new URL(rawFilePath, devUiUrl) (line 323) -> protocol allow-list (line 326) -> loopback check on targetUrl.hostname (lines 334-347) -> fetch(targetUrl.href, { signal }) (line 358) -> body returned to the caller (lines 370-371).
Why nothing on the path stops it: the loopback check only constrains the first hop and fetch follows redirects by default because no redirect: "manual" is passed, so a 3xx from the loopback dev server (the one host the check allows) is followed to any internal URL, including 169.254.169.254 and private ranges, and that internal response body is then sent back to the unauthenticated caller. The route performs no actor/authentication check at all, so the SSRF-capable proxy is reachable by anyone who can reach the port; only *writing* devUiUrl is gated (instance admin, server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1561-1566), *using* the proxy is not gated, and it is enabled whenever devUiUrl is set and NODE_ENV is not "production".
Impact: on any non-production deployment where a plugin author has configured devUiUrl for hot-reload, an unauthenticated attacker can use the server as a loopback proxy and read arbitrary paths from the developer's local dev server (Vite's /@fs/ handler, source files, any other localhost service bound to that port), and can pivot through a redirect from that dev server to cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) or other internal HTTP services and read their responses.
Fix: require a board actor for this route (at minimum for the dev-proxy branch), pass redirect: "manual" to fetch and either refuse 3xx responses or re-validate every redirect hop against the loopback allow-list before following it, and reject loopback targets that are not the exact configured dev server origin.

findings.title: Plugin SSRF via ctx.http.fetch reaches cloud metadata and private nets
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/services/plugin-host-services.ts:578 — hostServices.http.fetch, reachable from plugin worker code through ctx.http.fetch (packages/plugins/sdk/src/worker-rpc-host.ts:445, gated only by the manifest's http.outbound capability at packages/plugins/sdk/src/host-client-factory.ts:281,439).
Attacker: the author of an installed third-party plugin whose worker calls ctx.http.fetch with a URL of their choosing, crossing the boundary the host itself declares between plugin code and the host's private network/cloud metadata (the code comment says these are ranges "that plugins should never be able to reach").
Path: params.url -> validateAndResolveFetchUrl (line 111) -> protocol allow-list -> dns.lookup(hostname, { all: true }) (line 133) -> results.filter((entry) => !isPrivateIP(entry.address)) (line 150) -> first "safe" address pinned into the request via buildPinnedRequestOptions/executePinnedHttpRequest (lines 178-236).
Why nothing on the path stops it: isPrivateIP (lines 60-85) only covers 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16, 0.0.0.0, ::1, fc/fd prefixes, the literal fe80 prefix and ::. Addresses in 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598 shared/CGNAT space — which this product itself uses for private tailnet binding, e.g. PAPERCLIP_TAILNET_BIND_HOST=100.64.0.8 in cli/src/__tests__/network-bind.test.ts, and which contains the Alibaba Cloud metadata endpoint 100.100.100.200), 192.0.0.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 224.0.0.0/4 and 240.0.0.0/4 are classified as public, as are IPv6 link-local addresses whose compressed form does not literally start with "fe80" (fe90::/febf::) and IPv4-mapped forms written in hex (::ffff:7f00:1). Those results survive the filter, are chosen as safeResults[0], are pinned as the connection address, and the response is handed back to the plugin.
Impact: an installed plugin can read cloud instance metadata credentials (100.100.100.200) or reach services on the host's own private/tailnet range (100.64.0.0/10) that the host's fetch guard is explicitly meant to block, using nothing but ctx.http.fetch.
Fix: replace the string-prefix checks with CIDR matching over parsed addresses and cover the full reserved set (100.64.0.0/10, 192.0.0.0/24, 192.0.2.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4, 240.0.0.0/4, ::ffff:0:0/96, fe80::/10, ::/128, 64:ff9b::/96, 2002::/16), or better, restrict plugin fetches to an allow-list of hosts declared in the manifest and approved by the admin.

findings.title: Unauthenticated arbitrary file read via plugin UI entrypoint path traversal
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugin-ui-static.ts:228 (router.get("/_plugins/:pluginId/ui/*filePath")), reached from server/src/app.ts:276 where the router is mounted on the app with no board/actor check, so an unauthenticated network caller can call it.
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller who gets files from the host filesystem that neither the plugin bundle nor the anonymous web is supposed to expose, by riding on a plugin manifest value the host never bounds to the installed package.
The attacker requests GET /_plugins/<pluginId>/ui/<file>. pluginId resolves through registry.getById/getByKey (lines 247-259), the plugin is 'ready' and declares entrypoints.ui (lines 267-278), then the UI root is computed by resolvePluginUiDir (line 394): its node_modules branch does path.resolve(packageRoot, entrypointsUi) at line 155 with only fs.existsSync at line 158 — the containment check its own comment at line 157 claims ("and is actually inside the package") is not there, unlike the packagePath branch at lines 119-125 which at least does a startsWith test. `entrypoints.ui` is validated only as a non-empty string (packages/shared/src/validators/plugin.ts:400-403), so a manifest with entrypoints.ui = "../../../../" or "/etc" makes /, /etc, the server's cwd or the plugin install dir the containment root. The requested file is then resolved at line 411, and the traversal guard at lines 434-438 compares it against that root, so it passes, and line 481 sends it: res.sendFile(resolvedFilePath, { dotfiles: "allow" }) with "Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *" set at line 475.
Nothing on the path stops it: the handler performs no authentication or authorization at all (actorMiddleware in server/src/middleware/auth.ts only fills req.actor and calls next() for anonymous requests), the plugin package/manifest is third-party package data rather than operator configuration, the containment check is relative to the attacker-influenced root, and dotfiles are explicitly allowed so .env / .npmrc / .paperclip files are served rather than ignored.
Impact for this application: any file readable by the server process is downloadable by an unauthenticated caller — .env and config files holding the Postgres URL, LLM provider API keys and session secrets, the plugins' own configs, and other tenants' data on the same host — turning the plugin UI endpoint into an arbitrary file read with CORS open to every origin.
Fix: after resolving entrypoints.ui, require the resolved UI directory to be inside the resolved package root (and the package root inside localPluginDir) using realpathSync + path.relative containment (".."/absolute rejection), return null otherwise, and drop the string startsWith test in the packagePath branch in favour of the same realpath containment; additionally reject entrypoints.ui values that are absolute or contain ".." in the manifest schema, and serve only files inside that verified root.

findings.title: Unauthenticated plugin UI route serves dotfiles, leaking secrets
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugin-ui-static.ts:228 (GET /_plugins/:pluginId/ui/*filePath), mounted unauthenticated at server/src/app.ts:276.
Attacker: an unauthenticated remote caller who reads dot-files and secrets that live next to a plugin's UI bundle, because the sendFile options explicitly disable the dotfile protection that would otherwise hide them.
The request reaches res.sendFile(resolvedFilePath, { dotfiles: "allow" }) at line 481 after only the containment check at lines 434-438, which verifies the file is under the plugin's UI directory but says nothing about hidden files inside it; line 475 also sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on the response.
Nothing on the path stops it: the route has no authentication or authorization, the dotfile policy is turned off by the handler itself (the comment at lines 478-480 justifies it for Git worktree paths), and the only filter is containment, so any dotfile that ends up in the served directory tree — .env files, .npmrc with registry tokens, .paperclip plugin configs, editor/credential files copied into a built bundle, or the entire home directory when the UI root resolves outside the package (see the resolvePluginUiDir finding) — is returned verbatim to any caller.
Impact for this application: secrets that operators reasonably expect to be invisible to HTTP clients (dotfiles holding credentials, tokens and config) are downloadable without authentication and readable cross-origin, which is a direct sensitive-data exposure.
Fix: keep the traversal/root validation (see the resolvePluginUiDir finding) and serve with dotfiles: "deny" (or an explicit allow-list of file extensions under MIME_TYPES) so hidden files are never returned, and drop the wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin on this route.

findings.title: Non-admin board user can install plugins and gain instance-wide code execution
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:603 (POST /api/plugins/install; body packageName/version/isLocalPath).
Attacker: a board user who is only a member of one company (non-instance-admin) crossing from company-scoped access into instance-wide control and arbitrary code execution.
Path: assertBoard (line 604) -> loader.installPlugin({packageName|localPath}) (line 641) -> npm download or local path load -> registry/lifecycle.load -> app.ts:238-249 buildHostServices(pluginId, manifest) -> createHostClientHandlers with the manifest's declared capabilities, so the plugin worker runs out-of-process with instance-wide methods such as companies.list (plugin-host-services.ts:690-692, which returns every company) and http.fetch.
Why nothing stops it: the route only calls assertBoard, which merely requires req.actor.type === "board" (authz.ts:4-8); it never calls assertInstanceAdmin, even though that helper exists (authz.ts:10-16) and is used elsewhere in this very file to protect a much smaller concern (devUiUrl stripping at lines 1561-1566). The same assertBoard-only gate applies to enable, upgrade, delete and config routes. Plugin records have no company scope: ensurePluginAvailableForCompany is an explicit no-op (plugin-host-services.ts:492-497), and plugin capability approval is manifest-driven, so a company-scoped user can install a package whose manifest declares companies.read/http.outbound and immediately read all tenants' data or exploit the fetch path.
Impact: a non-admin, single-company user gains instance-wide code execution and cross-tenant data access, i.e. full privilege escalation beyond the boundary assertCompanyAccess enforces everywhere else.
Fix: require assertInstanceAdmin on install, upgrade, enable/disable, delete and config routes (and on any route that starts or restarts plugin workers), or introduce a per-instance plugin management permission and enforce it server-side.

findings.title: Invite test-resolution endpoint lets outsiders SSRF into internal network
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/access.ts:2103 (router.get("/invites/:token/test-resolution")), which passes req.query.url (access.ts:2115-2126) to probeInviteResolutionTarget (access.ts:1504) and fetches it here.
Attacker: an invited outsider (anyone who holds or obtains an invite link — the invitee is the untrusted external party the token is handed to), crossing from the public internet into the server's internal network and cloud metadata service.
The path: GET /api/invites/<token>/test-resolution?url=<attacker URL> -> invite looked up by tokenHash (only existence/revoked/expired are checked, access.ts:2106-2113) -> url parsed, only scheme restricted to http/https (access.ts:2118-2126) -> probeInviteResolutionTarget -> fetch(url, { method: "HEAD", redirect: "manual" }) at access.ts:1512 -> response status/duration returned to the caller at access.ts:2136-2142.
Why nothing stops it: the only gate on this route is the invite token itself (company invites are handed to external agents/people, and GET /invites/:token is a public route); there is no authentication, no allow-list of destination hosts, no rejection of loopback (127.0.0.1, ::1), private (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), link-local (169.254.0.0/16, incl. 169.254.169.254 metadata), or unique-local (fc00::/7) addresses, and no DNS re-resolution/pinning — undici resolves and connects to whatever host the query names.
Impact for this application: an outsider holding a single invite link turns the Paperclip server into an internal network scanner and reachability oracle (the JSON returns status reachable/timeout/unreachable, httpStatus and durationMs), letting them enumerate internal hosts/ports and probe the cloud metadata endpoint from inside the deployment, which is the first step of credential theft in hosted deployments.
Fix: before fetching, resolve the hostname and reject any loopback, private, link-local, multicast, ULA or metadata address (re-checking the resolved IP right before connect / pinning it to avoid DNS rebinding), or restrict the probe to the invite's expected gateway host; also consider requiring a signed-in board user for the probe rather than relying solely on the invite token.

findings.title: Race on board-claim lets two users both become instance admin
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/access.ts:1601 (POST /board-claim/:token/claim).
Attacker: a signed-in board user who holds the bootstrap claim URL (token+code leaked from the startup console/log), crossing from ordinary user to instance admin by racing the legitimate operator's claim.
Path: access.ts:1601-1619 reads token/code and calls claimBoardOwnership; board-claim.ts:89 calls getChallengeStatus, which only reads the in-memory activeChallenge and returns "available"; both concurrent requests then run the transaction at board-claim.ts:92-141, each inserting instance_admin for its own userId, deleting the local-board admin, and making that user owner of every company; the single-use flag claimedAt is written only afterwards at board-claim.ts:143-146, and even that write is a separate, non-atomic step.
Nothing stops it: there is no mutex, no atomic compare-and-set, and the DB transaction never touches the challenge state, so the "single use" guarantee is a check-then-act race; the second request is not rejected because claimedAt is still null while the first request is inside its transaction.
Impact: the one-time bootstrap capability can be redeemed more than once, so two different users can both become instance admins (and owners of all companies) even though the challenge is supposed to be consumed by exactly one claimant; an attacker holding a leaked/copied claim URL can still escalate while the legitimate operator claims.
Fix: make the consume-and-grant atomic - persist the challenge and consume it with a single conditional statement (e.g. UPDATE board_claim_challenges SET claimed_at = now(), claimed_by_user_id = $1 WHERE token_hash = $2 AND claimed_at IS NULL RETURNING id) inside the same transaction that inserts the instance_admin role, aborting if no row is returned; alternatively guard the in-memory check and flag with a lock held across the grant. Compare token and code with timingSafeEqual as well.

findings.title: Timing side channel in board-claim secret comparison leaks bootstrap token/code
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/access.ts:1590 (GET /board-claim/:token) and server/src/routes/access.ts:1601 (POST /board-claim/:token/claim).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller probing the public board-claim endpoints, crossing the boundary that protects the bootstrap secret by observing comparison timing.
Path: req.params.token and req.query.code / req.body.code reach inspectBoardClaimChallenge (access.ts:1595) and claimBoardOwnership (access.ts:1615), which call getChallengeStatus; board-claim.ts:36 compares activeChallenge.token !== token and line 37 compares activeChallenge.code !== (code ?? "") with JavaScript string inequality, which short-circuits on the first differing byte; the same non-constant-time comparison is repeated at board-claim.ts:143.
Nothing stops it: the endpoints are unauthenticated, return 404/409 on mismatch with different processing paths, and there is no rate limiting or constant-time comparison on the secret; the rest of the codebase (services/board-auth.ts:23-27, routes/access.ts:84-91) already uses timingSafeEqual for exactly this kind of check, so this path is the outlier.
Impact: a byte-by-byte timing oracle against the 12-byte claim code and 24-byte token; remote exploitation is impractical at these lengths over a network, but the single-use bootstrap secret that grants instance-admin is the one place where a constant-time comparison is required, and any reduction in the effective guessing space matters because the code is the only thing separating a signed-in stranger from instance admin.
Fix: decode both values to fixed-length buffers and compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual after a length check (or hash both sides with SHA-256 and use the existing tokenHashesMatch helper) in getChallengeStatus and at the claimedAt update.

findings.title: Cross-site POST promotes any user to instance admin via CSRF
findings.description: Entry: server/src/app.ts:169 (api.use(boardMutationGuard()) is the only CSRF defense for every /api route; the state-changing handlers are in server/src/routes/access.ts, e.g. POST /api/admin/users/:userId/promote-instance-admin at line 2897 and POST /api/companies/:companyId/join-requests/:requestId/approve at line 2597). Attacker: any website the operator visits, crossing from the public web into the local Paperclip instance's admin API (CSRF). Path: the default deployment mode is local_trusted (server/src/config.ts:169), so actorMiddleware stamps every request with {type:'board', userId:'local-board', isInstanceAdmin:true, source:'local_implicit'} without any credential (server/src/middleware/auth.ts:24-27); boardMutationGuard, the only Origin/Referer check for mutating /api calls, returns next() without checking Origin when req.actor.source === 'local_implicit' (server/src/middleware/board-mutation-guard.ts:53-58), so a cross-site POST with Origin: https://evil.example is accepted. Authorization is bypassed for the same actor as well (assertInstanceAdmin at access.ts:1583-1588 and routes/authz.ts:12; assertCompanyAccess at routes/authz.ts:25; assertCompanyPermission at access.ts:1816), and handlers such as promote-instance-admin (2897), join-request approve (2597), reject (2743) and invite revoke (2538) require no request body, so a simple form/fetch POST with a CORS-safelisted content type reaches them without a preflight. Nothing else checks a CSRF token - a repo-wide search finds no csrf middleware. Impact: a malicious page silently promotes an attacker-chosen user id to instance admin, approves a pending join request (onboarding an attacker's agent without the admin's consent) or revokes invites on the user's running instance. Fix: do not exempt local_implicit from the Origin/Referer check (the local UI is served from the same host, so its Origin would match trustedOriginsForRequest), or add a per-session CSRF token / SameSite-protected cookie for all mutating /api routes.

findings.title: Invite holders exhaust server outbound sockets via invite test-resolution probes
findings.description: Entry: server/src/routes/access.ts:2103 (GET /api/invites/:token/test-resolution, url and timeoutMs query params). Attacker: anyone holding a valid, unexpired invite token (an invited-but-untrusted agent/user or anyone given the invite link), crossing the boundary of the server's own outbound network/socket resources. Path: token is looked up at access.ts:2106-2113 (only revoked/expired invites are rejected, so the probe stays usable for the invite's full 10-minute TTL even after acceptance); req.query.url is parsed at 2115-2126 with only an http/https scheme check (no host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local/metadata block); req.query.timeoutMs is clamped at 2128-2134 to 1-15 seconds; probeInviteResolutionTarget then runs fetch(url, {method: HEAD, redirect: manual, signal}) at 1512-1516. Nothing on the path limits how many probes a caller can start or how long each one holds a connection: there is no rate limit, no concurrency semaphore, and the abort only fires after the attacker-chosen delay (up to 15s). Impact: an invite holder can issue many concurrent test-resolution calls pointing at an unroutable or slow address; each call keeps an outbound socket, a pending fetch and event-loop state alive for up to 15 seconds, so a burst exhausts the server's outbound connection/file-descriptor budget and degrades or stalls legitimate API traffic. Fix: restrict probe targets (deny private, loopback, link-local and cloud-metadata ranges, ideally allowlist expected webhook hosts), add a per-caller rate limit and a global concurrency cap for this endpoint, and use a small fixed probe timeout instead of a caller-supplied one.

findings.title: Non-CEO agent key can export the full company portability bundle via legacy /export
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/companies.ts:165 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/export).
Attacker: a non-CEO agent holding a valid agent API key for the company, crossing the CEO-only boundary the application itself draws for company portability exports.
Path: req.params.companyId and req.body enter the handler; validate(companyPortabilityExportSchema) only validates the payload shape; assertCompanyAccess(req, companyId) passes for any agent whose req.actor.companyId equals the company (middleware/auth.ts sets companyId from the agent API key) and for any board member with a membership; portability.exportBundle(companyId, req.body) is then called with no actor or role argument, so no role check happens anywhere on the path.
Why nothing stops it: the sibling routes POST /:companyId/exports/preview (line 203) and POST /:companyId/exports (line 210) both call assertCanManagePortability(req, companyId, "exports"), which throws unless the acting agent is the company CEO, and PATCH /:companyId/branding likewise requires the CEO role; the legacy /export route was left with the weaker company-membership check, so a general (non-CEO) agent key that the codebase deliberately denies on /exports can still obtain the full portable bundle through /export.
Impact: a low-privileged agent credential can exfiltrate the entire company portability bundle (company settings, agents and their adapter configuration, projects, issues and related records), which the application restricts to CEO agents.
Fix: replace assertCompanyAccess(req, companyId) in the /export handler with await assertCanManagePortability(req, companyId, "exports") (or delete the legacy route) so every export door enforces the same role policy.

findings.title: Agent API key can delete any issue and its attachment objects
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/issues.ts:1960 (DELETE /api/issues/:id).
Attacker: any agent holding a valid agent API key for the company, crossing the board/agent boundary that the same file enforces for other destructive issue operations.
Path: req.params.id is resolved to an issue via router.param and svc.getById; the handler then calls only assertCompanyAccess(req, existing.companyId) (which for agent actors just compares req.actor.companyId with the issue's company) and proceeds straight to svc.remove(id) plus storage.deleteObject for every attachment; there is no assertBoard, no permission-key check (such as tasks:assign used for assignment), and no per-actor ownership check.
Why nothing stops it: sibling destructive handlers in the same router are stricter, e.g. DELETE /issues/:id/documents/:key rejects non-board actors at line 1004 and POST/DELETE /issues/:id/read and /issues/:id/inbox-archive require req.actor.type === "board" at lines 1132, 1196 and 1228, so the codebase does distinguish board-only mutations; the delete route simply omits that check, and no service-level authorization compensates because issueService.remove takes only the issue id.
Impact: an automation credential can irreversibly destroy arbitrary issues and their attachment objects in its company (audit/activity history is written only after the deletion), which is a capability reserved for board users elsewhere in this file.
Fix: require board authentication (assertBoard(req), optionally gated on an instance-admin or explicit permission key) before svc.remove in this handler, matching the document-delete route.

findings.title: Hard-coded embedded PostgreSQL credentials give any local user superuser access
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/index.ts:351 and 371-375 (embedded PostgreSQL startup when no DATABASE_URL is set), whose credentials are reused at index.ts:413 and index.ts:419.
Attacker: any other local user or process on the same host (or in a container sharing the loopback interface) that can reach the embedded database port, crossing from "local unprivileged process" into the application's database and secret store.
Path: when DATABASE_URL is unset, the server starts EmbeddedPostgres with user: "paperclip" and password: "paperclip" and then builds the admin and application connection strings as postgres://paperclip:paperclip@127.0.0.1:<port>/... ; the same literal is compiled into the published package, so the credential is readable by anyone who reads the source and is identical on every deployment.
Nothing on the path stops it: the password is a fixed literal with no per-installation randomisation and no 0600 file like the secrets master key uses (server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:63-72); the database trusts password authentication, so a local attacker can connect as the superuser account, read/write every table including auth users, sessions, board API key hashes, company secret ciphertext and the verification records, and can insert rows to mint their own identity.
Impact: total compromise of the instance's stored identities and secrets from a local foothold, without needing any application-level credential.
Fix: generate a random password on first initialisation, persist it in a 0600 file alongside the data directory (or require an operator-supplied DATABASE_URL), and never ship a literal credential in source.

findings.title: Stored XSS: uploaded HTML asset served inline from app origin
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/assets.ts:110 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/assets/images), upload stored and later served by server/src/routes/assets.ts:312 (GET /api/assets/:assetId/content).
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent key that has access to a company, crossing into the browser session/origin of another user of that company, including an instance admin.
Path: the multipart file's client-supplied MIME type goes to assets.ts:141-145, where the SVG special-case is skipped for non-SVG types and isAllowedContentType() is called; server/src/attachment-types.ts:18-30 puts text/html in DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES and matchesContentType() accepts it exactly, so an HTML file is stored. On retrieval, assets.ts:322-331 sets Content-Type from the stored value, adds no Content-Security-Policy unless the type is exactly image/svg+xml (line 327), and always sends Content-Disposition: inline (line 331).
Nothing stops it: the allow-list check is the only gate and it deliberately admits text/html, the response is served with that exact Content-Type, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff does not prevent rendering a correctly typed HTML document, and the sandbox CSP is applied only to SVG. An attacker who is merely a member of a company can send the resulting /api/assets/<id>/content link to another member or to an instance admin (admins can access every company, so assertCompanyAccess passes for them), and the HTML runs as a same-origin document with the victim's session, letting it call every API the victim can call, including instance-admin routes.
Impact: stored XSS in the application origin, usable for privilege escalation from a low-privileged company member to instance admin and for reading/altering all data the victim can reach.
Fix: remove text/html (and other active types) from DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES, and in the asset content handler always send Content-Disposition: attachment for anything that is not a raster image, or send a strict sandbox CSP for every non-image content type instead of only for the exact image/svg+xml string.

findings.title: Stored XSS via SVG attachment whose MIME parameters bypass the sandbox CSP
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/issues.ts:2632 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/issues/:issueId/attachments), served by server/src/routes/issues.ts:2719 (GET /api/attachments/:attachmentId/content).
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent key with access to a company, crossing into another user's browser session in the application origin (including an instance admin who opens the attachment link).
Path: the multipart part's MIME type is taken verbatim at issues.ts:2665 via normalizeContentType() with no isAllowedContentType() check anywhere on this route (the only callers of that function are in assets.ts), and the raw bytes are stored. At retrieval, issues.ts:2729-2730 sets Content-Type to the stored string, issues.ts:2738 decides inline vs attachment through isInlineAttachmentContentType(), which matches by prefix ("image/*" matches "image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8"), while issues.ts:2734 applies the sandbox CSP only when responseContentType === "image/svg+xml" by exact string equality.
Nothing stops it: uploading an SVG with the part Content-Type "image/svg+xml; charset=utf-8" (a valid MIME type a Blob/FormData can carry) stores that exact string; the prefix match makes it inline, the exact-equality CSP check fails so no sandbox header is sent, and the browser renders the SVG document and executes its script. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff does not help because the declared type is a legitimate SVG type. An attacker who is a member of the company only needs to get another member or an instance admin to open the returned contentPath.
Impact: stored XSS in the application origin from a low-privileged company member to any user with access to that company, enabling session-wide API calls, secret management, and instance-admin actions as the victim.
Fix: enforce an explicit allow-list on attachment uploads, and in the content handler parse the media type (strip parameters) before both the inline decision and the CSP check, applying the sandbox CSP to all SVG types (and serving everything that is not a raster image as an attachment).

findings.title: Authenticated user can OOM shared server via unbounded GitHub import fetches
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/companies.ts:217 (router.post("/:companyId/imports/preview", validate(companyPortabilityPreviewSchema)) -> portability.previewImport(req.body) at line 226; the same path is reachable from companies.ts:172 POST /import/preview and companies.ts:233 imports/apply).
Attacker: any authenticated board user who is a member of a company (or a CEO agent on the agent-safe route), crossing the boundary of their own tenant by consuming the shared Node process's memory and outbound bandwidth, which can take the server down for every other tenant.
Path: req.body.source is parsed by portabilitySourceSchema (packages/shared/src/validators/company-portability.ts:185-187) as { type: "github", url: z.string().url() } with no host restriction; resolveSource (company-portability.ts:2751) calls parseGitHubSourceUrl (2690-2738) which checks only url.protocol === "https:" and then keeps url.hostname verbatim; the hostname flows into gitHubApiBase/resolveRawGitHubUrl (server/src/services/github-fetch.ts:8-17) and then into fetchJson/fetchText (company-portability.ts:2791, 2812, 2823) -> ghFetch (github-fetch.ts:19-25) -> response.json()/response.text(). Lines 2795-2808 build candidatePaths from every blob in the remote recursive tree with no cap on the count, and 2809-2815 issues one full-body fetch per path, storing every body in the single in-memory `files` record; fetchBinary at 2833 does the same with arrayBuffer() for the logo.
Nothing on the path stops it: ghFetch is a bare fetch with no AbortSignal and no timeout, fetchText/fetchOptionalText/fetchBinary/fetchJson (2187-2222) never inspect Content-Length or stream-abort on a size threshold, there is no per-file or total-byte budget and no limit on how many blobs are downloaded, and the only inbound protection is express.json({ limit: "10mb" }) (server/src/app.ts:118-124) which bounds the request body, not the size of the outbound responses. The private-hostname guard (app.ts:132-138) only gates the inbound Host header, and assertBoard/assertCanManagePortability (companies.ts:76-88, 217-231) check authorization, not cost.
Impact: a request of a few hundred bytes can make the server download an unbounded number of unbounded remote files (the attacker simply serves, or selects, a GitHub/GHE repository with a huge tree and huge .md files), holding all of it in one process; repeated or concurrent requests exhaust memory and OOM-kill the server, and the JSON parsing/manifest building over all of that content blocks the single event loop, denying service to all tenants.
Fix: allow-list the fetch host (github.com and the configured GHE hostname only) instead of trusting url.hostname, and re-validate after DNS resolution; give ghFetch an AbortSignal timeout and a maximum byte budget; stream each response and abort once a per-file and per-request total cap is exceeded; reject or truncate responses whose Content-Length exceeds the cap; and bound the number of tree entries fetched (and the size of the tree JSON itself).

findings.title: Cross-tenant secret disclosure via plugin secret-ref resolution
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1542 (POST /api/plugins/:pluginId/config, guarded only by assertBoard; the resolve RPC itself is server/src/services/plugin-secrets-handler.ts:261).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who is a member of company A only, crossing the per-company boundary to obtain the plaintext of company B's secret.
Path: the caller POSTs /api/plugins/:pluginId/config with configJson containing company B's secret UUID (as a declared format:"secret-ref" field, or as any UUID-shaped string when the plugin declares no instanceConfigSchema — extractSecretRefsFromConfig falls back to collecting every UUID, lines 122-162). The config is persisted instance-wide by plugin-registry.upsertConfig (no company scoping). When the plugin worker calls ctx.secrets.resolve(secretRef), the handler accepts the ref because it is now in cachedAllowedRefs (lines 289-309), then queries companySecrets with only eq(companySecrets.id, trimmedRef) (lines 314-318) — no companyId predicate — fetches the latest version material (lines 327-336) and returns provider.resolveVersion(...) plaintext (lines 345-351).
Why nothing stops it: the config route never calls assertCompanyAccess (plugin config is instance-wide), and the handler has no company parameter at all; it never compares secret.companyId to any company the caller belongs to. Every other secret path in this codebase (services/secrets.ts assertSecretInCompany, routines resolveTriggerSecret) enforces that match; this path deliberately omits it. The rate limiter, UUID format check and 30s config cache do not constrain which company the UUID belongs to.
Impact: cross-tenant secret disclosure. A user with access to one company can make any installed plugin with the secrets.read-ref capability resolve arbitrary other companies' secrets, and any plugin that uses a configured secret in an outbound request whose URL/headers are also attacker-controlled config values lets the attacker exfiltrate the plaintext. This bypasses the per-company restriction enforced on /companies/:companyId/secrets.
Fix: pass the acting company into createPluginSecretsHandler and require the resolved secret's companyId to be one the plugin is allowed to act for (or the caller's accessible companies); additionally require instance-admin for writing plugin config and/or for secret-ref fields, and validate that every secret UUID written into plugin config belongs to a company the caller can access.</br>

findings.title: Unsalted SHA-256 of every secret value enables offline cracking from DB dumps
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/secrets.ts:39 (POST /companies/:companyId/secrets), with the same path on POST /secrets/:id/rotate at server/src/routes/secrets.ts:69.
Attacker: a party who obtains read access to the secrets database or a database backup/replica (the DB is exactly the party the at-rest encryption does not trust), crossing the boundary AES-256-GCM encryption is supposed to draw between stored data and the plaintext secret values.
Path: the request body value passes validate(createSecretSchema) (or rotateSecretSchema), then secretService.create (server/src/services/secrets.ts:184) or rotate (:227) calls provider.createVersion, where localEncryptedProvider computes valueSha256: sha256Hex(input.value) at server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:127 using an unsalted, unkeyed, single-round SHA-256 (sha256Hex at line 75). services/secrets.ts then persists it into company_secret_versions.value_sha256 on every version insert (line 209 for create, line 237 for rotate), and packages/db/src/schema/company_secret_versions.ts:12/20 stores it as a NOT NULL, btree-indexed column.
Why nothing stops it: no guard, salt, key, iteration count, or KDF is applied anywhere on this path; the master key that protects the ciphertext is never used for this digest, and a grep of the whole repository shows valueSha256 is written but never read by any code, so the column has no functional purpose that would justify its exposure.
Impact: an attacker with only DB access (dump, backup, replica, or SQL access gained through another flaw) gets an offline verifier for every stored secret. Low-entropy values such as passwords, shared webhook secrets, and short tokens can be brute-forced cheaply, and any guessed value can be confirmed against the indexed hash; because the hash is unsalted and global, identical secret values are also linkable across companies and versions. This defeats the entire point of encrypting values with AES-256-GCM at rest.
Fix: stop computing and storing valueSha256 (drop the column and its index, since nothing reads it), or if an equality check is genuinely required, store a keyed HMAC-SHA-256 (or HKDF-derived subkey) of the value under the secrets master key so that a database-only attacker learns nothing and cross-tenant equality cannot be tested.

findings.title: Authenticated user can stall whole instance via unbounded adapterConfig.env bindings
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/agents.ts:833 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/adapters/:type/test-environment), which passes the caller-supplied body.adapterConfig into normalizeAdapterConfigForPersistence and then resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime (server/src/routes/agents.ts:838).
Attacker: an authenticated board user who holds only the agents:create permission on one company (assertCanReadConfigurations -> assertCanCreateAgentsForCompany, server/src/routes/agents.ts:234-249 and 827), crossing the tenant boundary by consuming instance-wide CPU, database connections and the single Node event loop that every other company shares.
Path: req.body.adapterConfig.env (a plain JSON object, bounded only by express.json's 10mb limit) -> normalizeAdapterConfigForPersistenceInternal (services/secrets.ts:151) -> normalizeEnvConfig, whose loop at services/secrets.ts:108 iterates every key of that object and calls assertSecretInCompany (services/secrets.ts:76-81) -> getById -> one SELECT per key; then resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime (services/secrets.ts:360-375) iterates the same keys again and calls resolveSecretValue (services/secrets.ts:83-97) -> assertSecretInCompany (another SELECT) + getSecretVersion (a second SELECT) + localEncryptedProvider.resolveVersion -> loadOrCreateMasterKey, which does a synchronous readFileSync of the master key on every single resolution (server/src/secrets/local-encrypted-provider.ts:53-55, 131-134) plus an AES-GCM decrypt.
Nothing on the path stops it: ENV_KEY_RE and envBindingSchema validate the shape of each entry but never the number of entries; assertSecretInCompany throws only for a secret that does not exist in the company, and the same valid secretId can be repeated for an unlimited number of distinct keys, so one self-created secret is enough to drive the loop; the 10mb body limit still admits roughly 100k+ secret_ref entries of ~50-90 bytes each; there is no per-request binding cap and no batching. One HTTP request therefore turns into ~300k sequential database round trips plus ~100k synchronous master-key file reads, all awaited on the single Node event loop.
Impact for this application: the server process stalls for minutes on one request (synchronous fs reads and sequential awaits block every other request, including other companies'), the Postgres connection pool is saturated, and the load is trivially repeatable in parallel, so a member of one company can take the whole instance offline.
Fix: cap the number of entries accepted in an env object (e.g. 100) and reject larger ones with 422 before any lookup; resolve bindings with a single batched query (WHERE secret_id = ANY(...)) instead of one query per key; cache the decoded master key in memory once per process instead of readFileSync per resolution; and enforce the cap in normalizeEnvConfig, resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime and resolveEnvBindings so every caller inherits it.

findings.title: HTTP adapter lets any tenant user SSRF the server into internal networks
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/agents.ts:1870 (PATCH /api/agents/:id, adapterConfig.url) and server/src/routes/agents.ts:1487 (POST /api/companies/:companyId/agents), consumed at server/src/services/heartbeat.ts:3677 via getServerAdapter(agent.adapterType).execute.
Attacker: any user with access to the company (board actor; assertCanUpdateAgent at routes/agents.ts:318-320 only checks company access) or an agent key acting on its own agent record (same function returns immediately when actorAgent.id === targetAgent.id), crossing from tenant/agent scope into the server host's internal network.
Path: adapterConfig.url -> svc.create/svc.update -> agent row -> heartbeat resolves it (resolveAdapterConfigForRuntime) -> adapter.execute({config}) -> `const url = asString(config.url, "")` (execute.ts:6) -> `fetch(url, { method, headers, body: JSON.stringify({...payloadTemplate, agentId, runId, context}) })` (execute.ts:19-27).
Why nothing stops it: the only checks on this path are `if (!url) throw` and the free-form adapterConfig record validator (packages/shared/src/validators/agent.ts:34, which only inspects `env`); there is no scheme allow-list, no host allow-list, no private/loopback/link-local check and no DNS pinning before the fetch, and `fetch` follows redirects by default so an external URL can bounce the POST to an internal one. The repository does contain exactly this defence for plugin HTTP fetches (isPrivateIP + validateAndResolveFetchUrl in server/src/services/plugin-host-services.ts:60-176), but the HTTP adapter never calls it.
Impact: the Paperclip server issues attacker-shaped requests (arbitrary method, headers such as Metadata-Flavor, arbitrary JSON body built from payloadTemplate plus run context) into loopback, RFC1918 and 169.254.169.254 endpoints, i.e. state-changing blind SSRF against internal admin APIs and cloud metadata services from a tenant-scoped caller, with run telemetry/logs leaking the target URL.
Fix: validate `config.url` before fetching - allow only http/https, resolve the hostname and reject loopback/private/link-local/ULA/0.0.0.0 and IPv4-mapped IPv6 (reuse isPrivateIP/validateAndResolveFetchUrl from plugin-host-services.ts), pin the resolved IP for the connection, set `redirect: "manual"` (or re-validate every redirect hop), and offer an operator-configured host allow-list for the http adapter.

findings.title: Cross-tenant data read via plugin bridge params.companyId
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:795 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/bridge/data")), authorization check at 829-831, worker call at 834-842.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A crossing into company B's data (cross-tenant IDOR).
The handler validates only the top-level body.companyId with assertCompanyAccess, then forwards body.params verbatim to the plugin worker's getData RPC. Plugin handlers read the company scope from params.companyId (the documented SDK pattern: packages/plugins/sdk/src/ui/hooks.ts:28-33 passes {companyId: context.companyId} in params, and the bundled example packages/plugins/examples/plugin-kitchen-sink-example/src/worker.ts:221 does `const companyId = typeof params.companyId === "string" ? params.companyId : ""` and then `ctx.issues.list({ companyId })`), and the host services those calls reach (plugin-host-services.ts:441) execute with the plugin's capabilities and no caller identity, so they return the requested company's issues/goals/agents. A caller therefore sends {companyId: "<company they belong to>", params: {companyId: "<victim company>"}}; the check passes on the first field while the plugin acts on the second. If the top-level companyId is simply omitted (line 829 is an `if`), assertCompanyAccess never runs at all.
Impact: any member of any company can read another company's issues, goals, agents and projects through any installed plugin that follows the documented handler pattern.
Fix: derive the company scope server-side (from the resolved plugin/actor) and pass it to the worker, rejecting any params.companyId that does not match the authorized company; make the company parameter mandatory rather than optional.

findings.title: Authenticated user can mutate another company's records via plugin bridge action params
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:878 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/bridge/action")), authorization check at 912-914, worker call at 916-925.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A crossing into company B's data and mutating it.
Same defect as the bridge/data route but on the write path: only body.companyId is checked with assertCompanyAccess, while body.params is forwarded untouched to the worker's performAction RPC, and plugin handlers take the company from params.companyId (packages/plugins/examples/plugin-kitchen-sink-example/src/worker.ts:478-508 uses getCurrentCompanyId(params) and then ctx.issues.create({ companyId, ... }) / ctx.issues.update(issueId, ..., companyId)). Nothing between the route and the host service re-checks the caller's membership, and the check is skipped entirely when body.companyId is absent.
Impact: a member of one company can create or modify records in another company (and trigger any other privileged plugin action) by supplying the victim company inside params.
Fix: resolve the acting company server-side, require it, and reject any params.companyId that differs from the authorized company before dispatching to the worker.

findings.title: Cross-tenant data read via unvalidated params.companyId in plugin getData proxy
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:962 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/data/:key")), authorization check at 995-997, worker call at 1000-1008.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A reading company B's data through a plugin (cross-tenant IDOR).
Identical to POST /plugins/:pluginId/bridge/data: the handler calls assertCompanyAccess on body.companyId only if it is present, then forwards body.params unchanged to the getData RPC, where plugin handlers resolve the company from params.companyId and query the host services with it. The top-level companyId can be omitted (skipping the check) or set to the attacker's own company while params.companyId names the victim.
Impact: any authenticated user can pull another company's issues/goals/agents/projects out of any installed plugin that follows the documented params.companyId convention.
Fix: compute the authorized company server-side and overwrite/validate params.companyId before the RPC instead of trusting the client-provided fields.

findings.title: Cross-company plugin actions via unvalidated companyId in params
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1041 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/actions/:key")), authorization check at 1074-1076, worker call at 1079-1088.
Attacker: an authenticated user with access to company A performing actions against company B's data.
The URL-keyed action route mirrors /bridge/action: assertCompanyAccess runs against body.companyId (and is skipped when that field is absent), while the worker's performAction handler reads the company from body.params (getCurrentCompanyId(params) in the bundled example) and then writes through host services that carry only the plugin's capabilities, not the caller's memberships.
Impact: cross-company writes and privileged plugin actions driven by any authenticated user of any company.
Fix: derive and enforce the acting company on the server, and reject params that name a different company.

findings.title: Board user can spoof agent identity to run agent-only plugin tools
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:519 (router.post("/plugins/tools/execute")), validation at 546-553, dispatch at 563-567.
Attacker: an authenticated board user crossing the agent boundary — executing plugin-contributed agent tools under a fabricated agent identity (agentId/runId chosen by the caller).
The whole runContext (agentId, runId, companyId, projectId) comes from the request body; the only authorization performed is assertCompanyAccess(req, runContext.companyId) (line 553), which merely proves the caller belongs to that company. Nothing verifies that agentId is an agent of that company, that it is not terminated/pending_approval, or that runId is a run of that agent; plugin-tool-dispatcher.ts:396-414 passes the object straight to the plugin registry/worker, where the plugin's tool handler treats runContext.agentId as the trusted caller identity. A board user who is only a member of company X can therefore invoke agent-only plugin tools as any agent of X (or of any company they can reach) and any audit/authorization decision a plugin makes on runContext.agentId is attacker-controlled.
Impact: agent-identity spoofing and invocation of plugin tools outside their intended agent-run context, defeating any per-agent restriction a plugin implements from runContext.
Fix: when the caller is a board actor, ignore the client-supplied agentId/runId (or require them to match a real, active agent of the authorized company and an existing run), and never treat request-body identity fields as authoritative inside plugin tool handlers.

findings.title: Any board user can read and overwrite instance-wide plugin secrets
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/plugins.ts:1542 (router.post("/plugins/:pluginId/config")), devUiUrl strip at 1561-1566, upsert at 1583-1585; the read twin is GET /plugins/:pluginId/config at 1512-1524.
Attacker: any authenticated board user (a company member with no instance-admin role) crossing into instance-level plugin secrets and configuration.
The route only calls assertBoard, then persists the caller-supplied configJson verbatim through registry.upsertConfig. The code itself acknowledges that board-level users are not trusted here — it strips devUiUrl for non-instance-admins because it "could be abused for SSRF" (comment at 1558-1560) — yet every other field, including secret values (API tokens, webhook signing secrets) that plugins rely on, is writable by any logged-in user; GET /plugins/:pluginId/config then returns the stored configJson to that same caller. Plugins are instance-global, and comparable instance-wide mutations require instance admin (authz.ts:10, instance-settings.ts:9-17).
Impact: a non-admin member of any company can read and exfiltrate instance-wide plugin credentials, or point a plugin's configuration at an attacker-controlled endpoint so its next run leaks data, without ever being an instance administrator.
Fix: require assertInstanceAdmin for plugin config reads and writes (at minimum for keys that hold secrets), or mark secret fields write-only and never return their values to non-admin callers.

findings.title: Authenticated user uploads HTML asset served inline, enabling stored XSS
findings.description:
Entry: server/src/routes/assets.ts:110 (POST /companies/:companyId/assets/images), content-type decision at line 141.
Attacker: any authenticated user or agent with access to the company, crossing the boundary from "can upload an image asset" to "can store script-capable HTML that is later served from the application origin" (the endpoint is named assets/images and its logo sibling only accepts image/*).
Path: multer parses the multipart part and exposes the client-declared Content-Type as file.mimetype (line 128); line 141 lowercases it and line 142 accepts it whenever isAllowedContentType returns true; that function matches against DEFAULT_ALLOWED_TYPES (server/src/attachment-types.ts:18-30, 84-91), which includes text/html, application/json and text/* by default, so a file declared as text/html is accepted and the raw HTML body is stored (line 146-167) with contentType = "text/html". The UI (ui/src/api/assets.ts:5-19) passes the browser's file.type straight through, so no client-side restriction compensates either.
Why nothing stops it: the MIME type is fully client-controlled and is never cross-checked against the bytes or the file extension (no magic-byte sniffing, no image decoding), and the default allow-list shipped in the code contains text/html; an operator only avoids this by explicitly overriding PAPERCLIP_ALLOWED_ATTACHMENT_TYPES. The only special handling is for image/svg+xml (sanitized at lines 147-154), while HTML is stored unchanged.
Impact: any company member or agent can plant an HTML document in the company's asset store; combined with the inline serving of GET /assets/:assetId/content (lines 322-331) this becomes stored XSS in the application origin and privilege escalation into the session of higher-privileged users who open the asset, and it also lets non-image content be presented as an image asset to every company member.
Fix: on this endpoint validate that the file is actually an image (magic-byte/decoder check) and reject anything outside an explicit image allow-list; stop using the environment-expandable attachment allow-list here and remove text/html and other script-capable types from the defaults used for inline-served assets.
